name: MathlibAnnex.Analysis.CStarAlgebra.Representation.isSimpleCStarAlgebra_of_singleton_of_injective
title: A faithful singleton model forces simplicity

content.display_title: A faithful singleton model forces simplicity
content.one_sentence_role: Uses irreducible representations annihilating proper ideals to rule out nonzero proper closed ideals.
content.natural_language_statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero unital complex $C^*$-algebra, and let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. Let $\pi:A\to\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital $*$-representation. Assume that $\pi$ is injective and is a singleton irreducible model among unital representations. Then every norm-closed two-sided ideal $I$ of $A$ is either $\{0\}$ or $A$.
content.assumptions: The singleton condition includes irreducibility on a nonzero space and unitary equivalence with every nonzero irreducible unital representation in the class of all complex Hilbert-space representations quantified in the definition. Injectivity is an explicit, separate hypothesis here. Neither $A$ nor $H$ is assumed separable.
content.conclusion: $A$ is simple in the sense of nontriviality and absence of nonzero proper norm-closed two-sided ideals.
content.proof_summary: An irreducible GNS representation kills a proper closed ideal. Transfer its zero action back through the singleton unitary, then use faithfulness.
proof_steps: Fix a closed two-sided ideal $I$. If $I=A$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise apply [A pure GNS representation annihilating a proper closed ideal](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/CStarAlgebra/State/Ideal.lean#L69-L94) with this proper closed $I$ in the nonzero ordered unital algebra $A$. It supplies a pure state $\varphi$ and an irreducible GNS representation $\rho:A\to\mathcal B(H_\varphi)$ with $\rho(a)=0$ for every $a\in I$. Its cyclic vector has norm one, so $H_\varphi\ne0$.

The singleton assumption, applied to this very $\rho$, gives a unitary $U:H\to H_\varphi$ such that $$U(\pi(a)x)=\rho(a)(Ux)\qquad(a\in A,\ x\in H).$$ If $a\in I$, the right side is zero. Injectivity of $U$ therefore gives $\pi(a)x=0$ for every $x$, hence $\pi(a)=0$.
Injectivity of $\pi$ and $\pi(0)=0$ yield $a=0$. Thus $I\subseteq\{0\}$ and $I=\{0\}$. Together with the first case and the given $A\ne0$, this is precisely the definition of simplicity.
